theme: Ordination of the priests, mediation established
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 29:1-46. This chapter describes the ceremony that sets Aaron and his sons apart as priests. It involves blood, ashes, and many animals, so read it slowly and ask what it says about how a person is made fit to serve a holy God.
settingTheScene: Chapter 28 described the priests’ clothing. Chapter 29 describes their ordination. It is a seven-day ceremony, and Leviticus 8 will tell how it was carried out. The rite involves washing, clothing, anointing, sacrifices, and the application of blood to the priests’ bodies. The point is that no one, not even Aaron, can serve in God’s presence simply because he wants to. He must be cleansed and consecrated by God’s own provision.
observation: The priests are washed with water at the entrance of the tent and then dressed in their garments (29:4-9).
Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the head of a bull, which is killed as a sin offering (29:10-14).
They lay their hands on a ram for a burnt offering, “a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD” (29:15-18).
Blood from the second ram is put on the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe of Aaron and his sons (29:19-21).
The priests are sprinkled with anointing oil mixed with blood (29:21).
The ordination lasts for seven days, with a sin offering each day for atonement (29:35-37).
The daily offering of a lamb each morning and evening is described (29:38-42).
God promises, “I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God” (29:45).
interpretation:
The ordination ceremony shows that the priests’ fitness for service is entirely a matter of God’s provision. Aaron does not earn the right. First he is washed. Then he is clothed. Then he is anointed. Then sacrifices are offered on his behalf, and he places his hands on the animals to identify himself with them. The priest is cleansed before he is allowed to cleanse others.

The laying on of hands is worth noticing. It is a sign of identification. When Aaron places his hands on the bull, the animal stands in his place. It is not a magic act. It is a picture of substitution: the animal’s life is given instead of the sinner’s. This is the first time you see this in detail, and you will see it again in Leviticus.

The blood on the ear, thumb, and toe is a striking detail. The priest’s hearing, his working hand, and his walking foot are all marked. It is a picture of a whole person given to God, set apart from head to toe for God’s service. The priest hears God’s word, does God’s work, and walks in God’s ways because blood has been applied to him.

The chapter ends with the promise that is the true goal of the whole system: “I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God. And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them” (29:45-46). The exodus was for this. God did not just release Israel from slavery. He brought them out so that he could live with them. The sacrifices, the clothes, and the priests are the means. His presence is the end.
connection: Hebrews contrasts the priests of the old covenant with Jesus. They were appointed “without an oath,” and they were prevented by death from continuing, but Jesus is a priest forever (Hebrews 7:20-24). Peter says that believers are “a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5), and the cleansing that makes this possible is Jesus’ blood (Hebrews 9:13-14). John writes that Jesus “made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father” (Revelation 1:6).
application:
Remember that you do not serve God because you are fit. You serve because you have been washed and clothed. Take that as encouragement if you feel unworthy.

Notice the ear, hand, and foot. Ask God to set apart what you listen to, what you do, and where you go for his glory.

Pray for pastors and ministry leaders you know, that they would serve out of grace and not out of pride.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for washing you and making you fit to serve.
Offer him your ears, hands, and feet, and tell him what you mean by it.
Ask him to make your whole life an offering.
